query: Consider the following context: Temper embrittlement, characterized by a dramatic loss of ductility within a narrow temperature window, is ubiquitous in conventional alloys but is not reported in compositionally complex or high‐entropy alloy systems. In that context, which material can be used for ductile–brittle–ductile transition, and why?

generation.hypothesis: A conventional tempered martensitic steel will display a ductile–brittle–ductile transition when thermally cycled through a narrow temperature window, because embrittling impurities segregate to grain boundaries only over this limited range.
generation.material_initial_state: Tempered martensitic steel with a homogeneous distribution of alloying and minor impurity elements resulting in ductile behavior at room temperature.
generation.intervention: Subject the alloy to controlled thermal cycles that span temperatures below, within, and above the expected embrittlement window.
generation.conditions: Experiments performed in an inert atmosphere with precise temperature control and mechanical testing (e.g., tensile tests and fracture toughness measurements) at various setpoints.
generation.structural_mediator: Grain-boundary segregation of embrittling species (e.g., phosphorus, antimony, tin) that momentarily compromises intergranular cohesion.
generation.mechanism: At intermediate temperatures the mobility of embrittling elements increases, leading to their preferential segregation at grain boundaries, which induces a brittle state. At temperatures outside this window, either segregation is insufficient (high temperature) or activity is frozen (low temperature), allowing the material to regain ductility.
generation.predicted_outcome: The steel will show high ductility at high and low temperatures, with a marked reduction in ductility and fracture toughness confined to a narrow, intermediate temperature range.
generation.baseline: Standard mechanical performance of tempered martensitic steel at room temperature without thermal cycling-induced segregation.
generation.boundary: This behavior is specific to conventional low/intermediate complexity alloys that allow impurity segregation; compositionally complex or high‐entropy alloys, which lack pronounced temper embrittlement, will not exhibit this transition.
generation.uncertainty: Exact transition temperatures and the magnitude of ductility loss depend on the precise impurity content and alloy composition, and variability in processing may affect the segregation behavior.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare samples of the tempered martensitic steel and subject them to a series of tensile and fracture toughness tests at temperatures incrementally spanning below, within, and above the presumed embrittlement window. Simultaneously, use microanalytical techniques (e.g., EDS, SIMS) to monitor impurity segregation at grain boundaries.
measurements: Tensile strength and elongation to failure at each test temperature
Quantitative analysis of grain-boundary impurity concentration
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the material does not exhibit a pronounced drop in ductility and fracture toughness confined to a narrow temperature range that coincides with increased grain-boundary impurity concentration, or if a similar transition is observed in compositionally complex alloys under the same conditions, the hypothesis will be falsified.
